facts.claim: "Piece of You" is the third of four tracks on hey, nothing's Maine release, runs 3:47, and came out June 21, 2024.
Maine was released by Good Luck Have Fun / Music Soup.
hey, nothing is the duo of Tyler Mabry and Harlow Phillips. They met in high school and cite Modern Baseball and Pinegrove as influences.
The duo is based in Athens, Georgia, and blends indie folk with pop-punk.
The Maine EP was written in a cabin in Maine.
Alt Press says the EP was recorded in Maine, in the sunroom of Phillips' grandmother's house.

Zillions Magazine describes "Piece of You" as aching with longing, a meditation on love that persists after it is gone. It describes the EP as an intimate meditation on addiction, heartbreak and change.
Phillips said the songs "Maine" and "The Sink" were the first the duo wrote formally together in a room. Before that they wrote separately.
Their 2023 debut album was We're Starting to Look Like Each Other, which leaned emo-flavored pop-punk. They released the 33° EP on Interscope in February 2025.

research.lineage: It sits in the emo-folk / Midwest emo and indie-folk tradition, a more rustic, acoustic turn from the duo's earlier emo-flavored pop-punk.

draft:
The house in **Piece of You** is a wreck, and the narrator is the one giving the tour. One verse locks the gates and swears not even a knock will get through. The next swings the door open: come in, look around, mind the shattered glass. "Watch your step, take your time" sounds like hospitality until you realize the guest is being walked through somebody's worst rooms and asked to take note of everything.

That pivot is the whole song. hey, nothing, the Athens, Georgia duo of Tyler Mabry and Harlow Phillips, wrote about wanting to be seen and dreading it in the same breath. "Let's see how much you can bear" is a dare, the kind people make so they won't have to ask whether someone will stay. The mirror waiting to fall, the vacant rooms and torn-up sheets, the flat admission that all they ever do is leave: it's damage laid out on purpose, by someone who seems half ready for the visitor to flinch so the ending gets decided early.

The chorus is where the guard slips. "There's a piece of you that I just can't ignore" sits right against a missing piece of the self, and the song never decides which loss cuts deeper. The bridge asks whether the visitor would rather go home to a life with open blinds and a warmer heart, then lands on a skull slammed into a wall. It's the most violent image in the song, and it comes framed as a question, almost as permission: you can leave.

The sound keeps all of this close. A bright, open strum of acoustic guitar carries it, with a plain bass line and drums settling into a steady, driving mid-tempo, snare on two and four. One clear, mid-range voice, no harmonies to share the weight. The recording is dry and a little raw, fitting for an EP written in a cabin in Maine and recorded in the sunroom of Phillips' grandmother's house there. After the emo-flavored pop-punk of their 2023 debut, We're Starting to Look Like Each Other, this is a more rustic turn, closer to Pinegrove, one of the duo's named influences. Their other cited touchstone, Modern Baseball, still shows in how bluntly the hurt gets said.

Zillions Magazine heard it as love that lingers after it's gone, and the last lines bear that out. Once the visitor is inside, the narrator claims to be free, with nothing left to see. That reads as relief and as emptiness, and the song lets both stand.

It sticks because it lets you walk through someone's wreckage as an invited guest, where the invitation and the warning to leave turn out to be the same gesture.

factCheck.claim: The 'bridge' asks whether the visitor would rather go home to open blinds and a warmer heart, then lands on a skull slammed into a wall

factCheck.claim: The narrator 'seems half ready for the visitor to flinch so the ending gets decided early'
factCheck.note: 'Ending' could read as a claim about the song's arc. Changed to 'the leaving'. The rest is interpretation.

factCheck.claim: Closing lines: the narrator claims to be free, with nothing left to see
factCheck.note: Matches 'Now you're in, now I'm free / There's nothing else for you to see'.
